facts.claim: UNESCO inscribed the Historic Centre of Warsaw as a World Heritage Site in 1980, recognizing its near total post-war reconstruction after more than 85 percent of the area was destroyed.
The Warsaw ghetto, established in October 1940, was the largest Jewish ghetto in German-occupied Europe, holding around 400,000 people at its peak.
The Warsaw Ghetto Uprising took place in April and May 1943, led by the Jewish Combat Organization under Mordecai Anielewicz, a distinct event from the general 1944 Warsaw Uprising.
POLIN Museum presents 1,000 years of Polish Jewish history through its core exhibition, which fully opened in 2014 on the former Warsaw ghetto site.
The Nozyk Synagogue, Warsaw's only synagogue building that survived World War II largely intact, opened in 1902 and was fully returned to the Warsaw Jewish community in 1983.
Chabad of Warsaw Poland operates a synagogue, kosher food services and a visitor center, with its own published guide to kosher dining options in the city.
Warsaw Chopin Airport's official site and the city transport authority list SKM rail lines, direct bus routes, licensed taxis and ride hailing apps as ground transport options to the city center.
Warsaw Modlin Airport, used mainly by budget carriers, is located well north of the city, and its official site lists dedicated coach connections to central Warsaw.
ZTM Warszawa coordinates an integrated network of metro, tram and bus service under the Warszawski Transport Publiczny brand, with a shared ticket valid across modes including the airport rail link.

The European Commission's Schengen visa policy lists Israel among the nationalities exempt from a visa for short stays of up to 90 days within any 180 day period across the Schengen area, of which Poland is a full member.
The European Union's official ETIAS travel authorization is expected to become a requirement for visa-exempt travelers in the last quarter of 2026, with a transitional period.
The Israeli embassy in Warsaw publishes its consular services and contact details through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs embassy portal.
Israeli travelers should verify Poland in the National Security Council travel warning system immediately before departure.

Official and independent climate data describe Warsaw's climate as moderately continental, with average temperatures below freezing in January and average highs roughly in the 20 to 26 degree Celsius range in July and August.
Wilanow Palace is a baroque royal residence built for King Jan III Sobieski in the late 17th century, now operated as a state museum with published palace and garden visiting hours.
The Fryderyk Chopin Institute operates the composer's birthplace museum in Zelazowa Wola, roughly an hour from Warsaw, including seasonal weekend piano recitals.

Kampinos National Park, a protected forest and dune landscape on Warsaw's northwestern edge, is recognized as a UNESCO biosphere reserve and maintains an extensive network of hiking and cycling trails.
PKP Intercity, Poland's main state rail operator, runs frequent trains between Warsaw and Krakow, with the fastest services covering the roughly 300 kilometer route in about two and a half hours.

The Warsaw Rising Museum, housed in a former tram power station in the Wola district, documents the 1944 Warsaw Uprising through photo archives, a database of participants and recorded oral history testimony.

Lonely Planet's guide to Warsaw organizes the city around districts including the Old Town, Southern and Northern Srodmiescie, Praga and the New Town, consistent with the neighborhood structure used throughout this guide.
